guidance:
Use only Table 1 to define structure and values. Ignore narrative text and footnotes as data sources.

1) Table scope and title
- Set `table_title` to the caption of Table 1, copied verbatim.
- Work strictly within the visual bounds of Table 1; do not mix in material from other tables or figures.

2) Columns and headers
- Rebuild the header region from left to right before creating any cells.
- Include every explicit data column header in `columns` (groups/arms, timepoints, statistics such as effect size, p value, etc.).
- For multi-row or nested headers, treat only the lowest-level headers as data columns. Create each `column_label` by combining the higher-level and leaf text into a single string (e.g., "Top: Leaf"). Do not add the grouping header alone as a column.
- The leftmost label column may have its own heading. If it has a name, include that heading string in `columns`, but never create data cells for it; its contents are represented via `row_group` and `row_label`.
- Every `column_label` used in any cell must appear exactly once in `columns`. Do not invent additional columns (such as totals or combined groups) unless they appear as distinct header cells.

3) Row structure: row_group and row_label
- Read down the first column and distinguish:
  • Section/category headings: visually distinct, often spanning multiple columns or followed by a block of related rows.
  • Data rows: aligned with values in one or more data columns.
- Use each section/category heading as `row_group` for the data rows it clearly governs. For those rows, the text in the leftmost column is `row_label`.
- Rows that are not under any clear heading use `row_group` = null.
- If a section heading itself has data values on the same line, represent that line with `row_group` equal to the heading text and `row_label` = null.
- Do not swap roles: `row_group` is the broader category or section; `row_label` is the specific item within that category. Do not place item text in `row_group` or section text in `row_label` for the same data.
- If the same heading or item appears more than once, reuse the exact wording so grouping stays consistent.

4) Cells and values
- A cell corresponds to one non-empty intersection of a data row and a data column.
- For every visible entry in the body (numbers, text, symbols), create exactly one object with `row_group`, `row_label`, `column_label`, and `value`.
- Copy each `value` verbatim, including spaces, punctuation, parentheses, ranges, units, percent signs, plus/minus signs, and textual markers such as N/A-like text or dashes when they appear as values.
- A printed zero is a real value and must be captured.
- Do not create cells for blank table positions and do not infer or calculate values.

5) Avoid missing, extra, and duplicate cells
- Work row by row. For each data row, scan across all data columns in the header and add one cell for every non-empty entry; do not add cells where the table cell is blank.
- Do not create cells for pure header or section lines that have no data values in the body.
- Do not move values between categories or columns, and do not add derived totals or combined values that are not explicitly printed in the table.
- Each combination of (`row_group`, `row_label`, `column_label`) must be unique. Never emit more than one cell for the same position.

6) String consistency
- Use table wording verbatim for `table_title`, `columns`, `row_group`, `row_label`, and `column_label`, preserving spelling, capitalization, spacing, and symbols.
- Confirm that every `column_label` appearing in `cells` matches exactly one entry in `columns`, and that identical headings used as `row_group` are written identically wherever they occur.
